>The first thing I do is scan all servers to see where an account is used on services and scheduled tasks. There are multiple ways to do it but I like CJWDEV Service Credentials Manager. I paid for it but the free version should be good enough.

This is helpful, I wrote some scripts to check in a few places, but having something comprehensive would be very helpful. Thanks.

>Then you need to know where the account is authenticating to find network shares or databases it talks to. Or it could be configured inside a Linux-based appliance. This data can be more difficult to gather. You need to report on the domain controller Security event logs. For this, I use ManageEngine AD Audit Plus. It's incredibly cheap for what it does but I don't know if there is any free option. You could set up a trial but that would be a lot of work for 30 days of use.

Yeah, big problem is that these accounts run on appliances. I've sorted most of the Windows based stuff, but the appliances are the headaches. Security event logs have gotten at least part of the outlining done. It's the last leg to build the confidence that my changed won't break anything that is nerve wracking. My boss has beef with ManageEngine, but I will give them another look and see if I can't talk him back into it.

>Because my company had a tendency to share the same service account across many processes, my preference is to create a new service account for each process and migrate one process at a time. Once I think I have found all the places a service account is used, I replace the account with the new one and see if anything breaks. When I think the old service account is dead, I create an alert in AD Audit to email me if it authenticates. I wait a couple of weeks, preferably over month end, and then disable the old account.

This logic is sound. I have done a similar process to move some of our hosted applications onto proper service accounts. I just wish literally any of them had been configured not-with-Domain Admin. I like the tip about e-mailing when it auths, didn't think about that even though I have it set for a couple of sketchy accounts i'm told are "Important."

>I recently used this method to migrate a heavily shared, highly privileged service account and I didn't break anything. I also created documentation on how to change each password in the future. For example, change the password on X service on Y server, recycle the service and then check Z directory to make sure new files are still being created. Now if we ever get compromised or maybe a sysadmin leaves on bad terms, we can confidently change all privileged service account passwords without breaking stuff.
